question: What is the simplest approach to achieve both test-time scaling and strong reasoning performance?
hypothesis: Pretrained models already hold reasoning ability, so SFT on a small, difficult, diverse, high-quality set (1,000 samples) plus a decoding-time control of thinking length suffices.
contributions: s1K: 1,000 questions with reasoning traces selected by difficulty, diversity and quality (§2)
budget forcing, a decoding-time test-time scaling method (§3)
s1-32B, competitive with o1-preview, the most sample-efficient open-data reasoning model (§4)
ablations of data selection (§5.1) and test-time scaling methods (§5.2); Control/Scaling/Performance metrics (§3.2)

method.summary: SFT of Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on s1K (1,000 questions, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking traces) gives s1-32B. At inference, budget forcing caps thinking by appending the end-of-thinking delimiter, or lengthens it by suppressing that delimiter and appending 'Wait'. Compared against conditional length control and rejection sampling.
method.task: supervised fine-tuning for reasoning plus test-time compute scaling (math and science QA)

training.objective: next-token prediction (SFT); loss only on reasoning trace and solution, not on the question
training.lr_schedule: cosine decay to 0 over remaining 299 steps
training.compute: 7 H100 GPU hours (59K run: 394 H100 GPU hours)

other.delimiters: thinking enclosed by <|im_start|>think and <|im_start|>answer, each preceded and followed by a newline
other.seq_len_32768: inferred: Table 8 Model B training sequence length 32768, 0% cutoff; text says only 'longest training sequence length'

inference.decoding: greedy; vLLM; budget forcing appends end-of-thinking delimiter (optionally 'Final Answer:') to cap, suppresses delimiter and appends 'Wait' to extend
inference.temperature: 0 unless stated; 1 for majority voting (64 evals) and rejection sampling
inference.max_tokens: about 30,000 thinking tokens max for Table 2 scores
inference.samples: 1 greedy run per benchmark; majority voting 2..64 samples (Fig 4b); REBASE and majority 16 trajectories (Fig 7); Table 3 uses |A| = 2 to 5 evaluation runs per method
inference.prompting: questions as-is; length-control variants add instruction to user prompt (Fig 10)

other.determinism: Scores vary across runs even with same seed and greedy (batch size, tensor parallelism, continued generation); final evals mostly in full precision

metrics.name: Control
metrics.definition: fraction of runs whose thinking tokens fall within a_min..a_max

metrics.name: Scaling
metrics.definition: average slope of piece-wise linear accuracy vs thinking tokens
metrics.unit: accuracy points per compute unit (not stated)

eval.protocol: Own runs for s1 variants, Qwen and Gemini (AIME24 only, via web interface because of API recitation error); others from reports. 95% paired bootstrap CIs (10,000 samples) for differences relative to s1K in Table 2.

prompts.purpose: grading prompt for correctness of attempts
prompts.text: You are an AI assistant for grading a science problem. The user will provide you with the question itself, an attempt made by a student and the correct answer to the problem. Your job is to judge whether the attempt is correct by comparing it with the correct answer. If the expected solution concludes with a number or choice, there should be no ambiguity. If the expected solution involves going through the entire reasoning process, you should judge the attempt based on whether the reasoning process is correct with correct answer if helpful. [format: # Problem {problem} ## Attempt {attempt} ## Correct answer {solution}] Explain your reasoning, and end your response on a new line with only "Yes" or "No" (without quotes).
Answer after a short amount of thinking. Do not spend excessive time double-checking your work.
Answer after a long amount of thinking. If you feel like you are finished early, spend the extra time trying to double-check your work until you are absolutely sure that you have the correct answer.

limits: Budget forcing flattens out and is bounded by the context window (§6.2).
Single greedy runs on 30-problem AIME24; evaluation not deterministic across batch size or parallelism (App B), so 2-3 point differences are within noise.
Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking was evaluated on AIME24 only, via web interface; MATH500 and GPQA are N.A.
Only about half of s1K traces are correct per the grader (53.6%).
Data filtering used the same base model (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) that is fine-tuned; authors say the idea should generalize, not shown.
Open question whether r1-level performance is reachable with 1,000 samples.
Fig 7 step-conditional model used an earlier data version and eval codebase.
